overview: The atlas calls this broad patch “Shellfish gatherers,” but that is an economic label, not a people's name. Its polygon follows parts of southeastern and southern Brazil while sweeping inland. Archaeologists call local shell sites sambaquis, a later Tupi-derived term. They were far more than clam-dinner heaps. Layers can contain fish bones, plants, hearths, tools, ornaments and burials; enormous mounds became landmarks of memory. Fish often supplied more protein than shellfish, while dental calculus, teeth and stone tools reveal important plants. Communities around Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná and Santa Catarina did not form one timeless culture, language or government. Genomes likewise reveal regional diversity and later contact despite similarities in mound building. Near this card's final centuries, some sites changed from shell-rich layers to darker fish-rich deposits, and pottery appears in particular contexts. The atlas polygon narrows sharply in 800 and disappears in 900. Those are map seams, not proof that coastal families vanished. Distinct Indigenous peoples live across these regions today, and no living nation should be treated as the automatic name or voice of every ancient mound builder.

periods.title: 1500 to 1000 BCE: an atlas label meets older local histories
periods.summary: The target begins as one polygon over coast and inland, although Brazilian shellmound traditions began much earlier and varied regionally. Cabeçuda dates require correction because marine foods can make human bone appear too old. Display dates therefore organize the card; they do not create one archaeological phase.

periods.title: 1000 to 700 BCE: mounds grow beside changing water
periods.summary: Around lagoon systems, repeated building, burial and gathering made prominent places across generations. Shorelines were never fixed: bays became lagoons, dunes moved and sediments accumulated. Researchers reconstruct each setting from cores, dates and site position rather than assuming today's beach marks the ancient waterline.

periods.title: 700 to 500 BCE: plants complicate the seafood stereotype
periods.summary: Dental disease, isotopes and microscopic plant remains at Babitonga Bay point to substantial carbohydrate foods and possible cultivation in some communities. That evidence is local, and the domestication status of several plants remains uncertain. “Shell mound” describes construction material better than a complete menu.

periods.title: 500 to 200 BCE: monuments, cemeteries and homes differ
periods.summary: Jabuticabeira II preserves repeated funerary activity, while nearby smaller sites had different formation histories. Shell, dark sediment, fish bone, ash and posts must be read layer by layer. Similar mound shapes do not prove identical function, family organization or belief along the entire coast.

periods.title: 200 BCE to 100 CE: contact does not erase regional identity
periods.summary: Ancient DNA shows coastal groups were genetically heterogeneous even when parts of their archaeological record looked similar. Genetics can test ancestry and contact, but cannot name a person's language or nation. Tiny atlas coordinate changes around 100 and 1 BCE add cartographic precision, not biological events.

periods.title: 100 to 300 CE: repeated rites build social memory
periods.summary: At Jabuticabeira II, fish-rich layers, hearths and burials support an interpretation of repeated funerary meals and memorial acts. The mound grew through many events rather than one construction project. A feast can reinforce relationships, but its remains cannot identify every guest or exact prayer.

periods.title: 300 to 500 CE: shorelines and fisheries keep changing
periods.summary: Lowering sea level, sand barriers and lagoon silting could alter salinity and access to shellfish or fish. A sambaqui's elevation is not a simple ancient tide gauge because people selected and modified locations. Archaeological and geological evidence must be modeled together.

periods.title: 500 to 700 CE: late sites show continuity and encounters
periods.summary: Southern coastal routes linked older mound places, fish-rich deposits and communities associated with new pottery. Archaeologists find both continuity and change in diet, architecture and technology. Pottery does not automatically prove a complete population replacement, and one encounter model cannot cover every bay.

periods.title: 700 to 800 CE: bodies record work and health unevenly
periods.summary: Bones and teeth preserve diet, injury, infection and repeated activity, but collections differ in preservation and excavation history. Regional studies reject the idea of universally fragile or universally peaceful shellmound people. In 700 the atlas still shows the broad polygon, one editorial snapshot among local histories.

periods.title: 800 to 900 CE: the map contracts, then removes its umbrella
periods.summary: In 800 the target is clipped to a smaller southern piece, and at 900 it disappears. Late coastal sites can retain marine diets and mound-like funerary architecture while shells diminish and ceramics appear. This is transformation and encounter, not a synchronized disappearance of coastal peoples.

sections.title: Read the economic label and archaeological evidence carefully

items.text: “Shellfish gatherers” is the atlas editor's category, not a recovered self-name. It risks reducing people to one ingredient. The card retains the exact id for software compatibility while treating each mound, bay and dated community separately. Fishing, plants, hunting, ceremony, construction and exchange all belonged in the wider picture.

The early polygon follows the Atlantic coast from around Rio de Janeiro toward Santa Catarina, yet its northwestern edge cuts far inland. Its boundary excludes some famous eastern Rio shellmound areas while including interior cities. That geometry cannot be a surveyed ethnic, language or archaeological frontier.

Soil micromorphology at Rio Preto I separates shell deposits, burning, organic movement and later soil formation. This matters because roots, animals, rain and chemistry alter a mound after people leave. Archaeologists do not simply count visible shells; they study thin sections, elements, layers and radiocarbon context.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none represents this exact atlas umbrella. Original script: unavailable. Transliteration: unavailable. Translation: unavailable. “Sambaqui” is a later Tupi-derived archaeological term, not a surviving sentence written by these builders. Rich speech and oral knowledge certainly existed, but no secure text identifies their languages.

Small inland shellmounds in the Ribeira highlands have different materials, foods and chronologies from monumental coastal sites. Capelinha diet evidence is terrestrial despite shell and coastal connections. Shared shell construction can signal contact or similar choices without proving one ancestry, political system, language or migration route.

sections.title: Build landmarks in moving lagoons, dunes and estuaries

items.text: Ground-penetrating radar beneath a southern mound found archaeological layers over an old lagoon margin and wind-built sediments. The method maps contrasts without digging away the whole site. It helps reconstruct why a once-watery edge may now look dry, inland or buried beneath later landscape change.

A mound's shells could be food remains, building material, grave covering or several things at different moments. Human isotopes sometimes disagree with what the most visible shells suggest. The useful question is not “trash heap or temple?” but which activities built each layer and how they changed.

Araujo II in Paraná contains stratified shell, ash, stone and bone objects and burials. Recreio, beyond the polygon's southern edge, preserves a separately dated coastal sequence. Older excavations remain valuable, but a layer is not a calendar page unless its context stays intact.

Late southern routes connected mound sites, discrete camps and Jê-associated contexts across wetlands, dunes and higher ground. Least-cost paths are models of possible movement, not footprints. They help compare terrain and access while leaving room for boats, seasonal water, social permission and routes archaeologists cannot recover.

Many sambaquis were quarried for lime, damaged by construction or exposed by erosion. IPHAN protects archaeological heritage, while museums preserve collections and site records. Conservation is an achievement in the present because a mound cannot be re-excavated after bulldozing, and an unlabeled box can lose nearly as much history as a destroyed layer.

sections.title: Eat fish, shellfish, plants and terrestrial foods in varied proportions

items.text: Isotope models at Piaçaguera and Moraes show different mixtures of marine, freshwater and terrestrial foods, plus differences among individuals. The numbers are estimates shaped by baseline animals and tissue turnover. They defeat the idea that every mound builder ate the same seafood plate merely because shell preserves spectacularly.

At Morro do Ouro, cavities, bone chemistry and plant microremains point to carbohydrate-rich foods. Possible yam, sweet potato, palm and other plants appear, but identification and domestication status need caution. Tropical plant foods often vanish unless charred or trapped in dental calculus, making the surviving shell pile an unfairly loud witness.

Ilha Grande fish assemblages represent reef, estuary and open-water habitats, while thousands of bone artifacts help test capture methods. Species lists can reveal seasonal and environmental choices, but fish bones also reflect screen size, preservation and which parts reached the mound. Fishing skill was ecological knowledge plus technology.

Mollusk shells identify habitats and collection choices, but people may have carried shell for building as well as food. Tarioba biodiversity research uses many species to reconstruct coastal conditions. A giant mound is therefore not one enormous restaurant receipt; it is a time-layered human construction with ecological clues.

Marine mammals, birds and reptiles contributed meat, bone, teeth and symbolic materials at southern sites. Zooarchaeologists examine species, cut marks, burning and artifact manufacture before deciding how an animal was used. A whale bone tool does not by itself prove the animal was hunted rather than found stranded.

sections.title: Engineer fishing gear, stone tools, containers and art

items.text: Saquarema Lagoon sites east of much of the decoded polygon provide a labeled regional comparison: worked fish spines and bone points represent different fishing technologies. Their exact targets remain debated. Similar-looking points elsewhere require local wear, context and fauna before researchers assume the same technique or cultural identity.

At Camboinhas, researchers identify fish more precisely and ask how bodies were processed. The site lies outside or near the map's northeastern seam, so it cannot silently stand for the entire target. It is useful comparison showing how better taxonomy changes stories about capture, season and disposal.

Prainha stone artifacts preserve an operational sequence: choosing raw material, shaping edges, using tools and sometimes reworking them. A finished ax hides those steps. Reconstructing the chain shows planning and learned technique, while no stone flake tells us whether the teacher was a parent, specialist or patient friend.

Grinding stones, mortars and dental microremains make plants technologically visible. Processing could crush fibers, nuts, roots or seeds, but tool form alone does not name a recipe. Different residues and wear patterns matter. Food technology included knowledge of what decays, even when museums end up displaying mostly durable stone and shell.

Southern sites produced polished stone or bone animal sculptures called zooliths, as well as ornaments and practical tools. Their realism can delight children, but an animal-shaped bowl is not a captioned myth. It demonstrates design, patient grinding and shared conventions while its spoken story remains unknown.

sections.title: Organize living space, fires, water and waste without inventing plumbing

items.text: Postholes, hearths and activity deposits imply built spaces, yet tropical wood, thatch and fiber usually decay. Geophysical survey can find buried features without exposing them all. The evidence supports shelters and planned activity areas, not one standard house drawing for every coastal region and century.

Microscopic charcoal anatomy identifies woods burned in funerary areas and distinguishes some depositional sequences. Fire supplied heat, light, cooking and material transformation, but a charcoal fragment needs context before becoming a domestic hearth. Smoke management, fire tending and fuel collection were learned household work even when roofs disappear.

Shell beads and ornaments placed with a child at Cabeçuda show adornment and careful mortuary treatment. They do not preserve a full wardrobe. Plant fiber, hide and feathers may have served clothing or carrying needs but rarely survive; the honest card avoids dressing everyone in one speculative costume.

Lagoon water could be salty or brackish, so communities still needed reliable fresh drinking water. Site location, hydrology and containers matter, but no reviewed source documents one umbrella-wide well or plumbing system. Changing barriers and sediment could alter water access within a family's lifetime.

No reviewed excavation identifies a shared toilet, latrine or sewer. Mounds contain food refuse, ash, broken objects, human burials and deliberate construction layers, sometimes carefully separated. That organization is evidence for spatial rules, but calling any dark patch a bathroom would be funny for the wrong reason and scientifically reckless.

sections.title: See households, women, age groups and cooperation without stereotypes

items.text: At Corondo, east of the polygon's strongest coastal core, grave goods were interpreted as showing differences by age, gender and status, including changing female prestige. This is one mortuary study, not a constitution for all sambaqui societies. Burial treatment can express identity without mapping daily authority exactly.

A broader Rio de Janeiro review found burial goods were not exclusively assigned to one gender, even when some tendencies appeared. That warns against labeling fishing points “men's tools” or plant equipment “women's work” by habit. Bones may estimate biological sex; objects do not automatically reveal gender identity or job.

Funerary contexts vary so much that researchers use gender as a question rather than a ready answer. Women, men and people whose identities do not fit modern binaries all require evidence-based treatment. The safest conclusion is social diversity, not an invented universal division of coastal labor.

Repeated burial clusters and meals at Jabuticabeira II suggest groups returned to honor particular dead and renew relationships. Archaeologists may discuss affinity groups, but a burial cluster is not automatically a biological family. Adoption, marriage, friendship and ritual belonging cannot be read from proximity alone.

Building a visible mound required coordinated carrying, fishing, gathering and ceremony across generations. That is a social achievement. It does not prove enslaved labor, a king or compulsory taxation. Regional reviews debate hierarchy and heterarchy because cooperation, prestige and inequality can coexist without a centralized state.

sections.title: Follow babies, children, learning and play through careful clues

items.text: Isotopes from Jabuticabeira II suggest supplementary foods began near six months for sampled children and complete weaning often occurred around two to three years. These are modeled averages from particular bones and teeth, not parenting instructions or a fixed rule. Feeding a child joined biology with family care and available foods.

Growth disruptions and bone lesions at Jabuticabeira II show that some children experienced physiological stress or infection, while survival to later ages records resilience and care. Skeletal stress is not a report card on parenting. Disease, food, environment and preservation interact, and the sample represents people who were buried there.

A carefully ornamented child's burial at Cabeçuda makes childhood visible without reducing the young person to an age category. Shell adornments show investment and remembrance. They cannot tell whether the child wore them in life, who made them, or what words mourners spoke beside the grave.

Children probably learned knots, balance, tide timing, plant recognition and tool safety through watching and helping, but no excavated object is automatically a lesson. A small point might be practice, a finished tool or a broken adult object. Production sequences reveal skill levels more securely than invented schoolrooms.

The Joinville museum teaches with tens of thousands of artifacts and protects knowledge recovered from damaged sites. Modern museum learning is not an ancient classroom, yet it makes a good continuity lesson: asking, drawing, comparing and caring for context are skills too. Archaeology has no secure sambaqui board game or recess schedule.

sections.title: Investigate health, medicine, food safety and hygiene without diagnosis games

items.text: High cavity rates at Morro do Ouro support substantial carbohydrate consumption, while neighboring groups show different patterns. Teeth preserve diet and disease together. A cavity does not identify one plant or prove poor hygiene; texture, processing, mouth bacteria, age and sampling all matter.

Ancient DNA from Jabuticabeira II reconstructed treponemal bacteria related to diseases in the same family as syphilis, but the genomes represent an ancient non-venereal lineage. Researchers combine lesions, molecules and dates rather than diagnosing from appearance alone. Pathogen history is not a reason to stigmatize the buried community.

Jabuticabeira II children show non-specific stress indicators, which can form after many kinds of hardship. They do not name a fever, famine or treatment. Evidence of survival may imply feeding and caregiving, yet the bones cannot identify a healer, medicine bundle or exact household response.

Cabeçuda and Arapuan samples showed low observed levels of trauma interpreted as interpersonal violence, but sample sizes and preservation limit the conclusion. Low injury prevalence is not proof that conflict never happened; it simply rejects a cartoon of constant fighting and demands local, dated evidence.

No securely attributable medical recipe survives for this umbrella. Plant remains may represent food, fuel, offerings or medicine, and healed bones can show recovery without naming treatment. Clean water, waste placement, fire and food processing affected health, but no single hygiene code can be reconstructed from shell layers.

sections.title: Honor burials and beliefs without translating silent objects

items.text: At Jabuticabeira II, repeated fish-rich feasts and burials helped construct the mound. Meals may have joined mourners and ancestors, but archaeologists infer ceremony from patterned deposits rather than a written liturgy. One cemetery's sequence should not become the religion of every mound along two thousand kilometers of coast.

Carbonized seeds and palm nuts in funerary features could be feast remains, offerings or both. Charring improves survival, so preserved plants are a biased sample of everything used. Their position beside hearths and burials narrows possibilities without providing the name of a spirit, dish or ritual specialist.

Thousands of fish otoliths, the hard “ear stones” that help fish balance, occur in Jabuticabeira II funerary contexts. Researchers ask whether some were selected beyond food disposal. Fun fact: a tiny fish balance stone can become a human clue, but it still does not whisper its meaning to archaeologists.

Burial goods and body treatment vary across Rio de Janeiro sites. Some patterns relate imperfectly to biological sex or age, while none supplies a universal gender rule. Respectful interpretation keeps biological estimates, social gender, personal identity and archaeologists' own assumptions from collapsing into one label.

Mound scale proves sustained work, not the political method used to organize it. No palace archive records orders, and no laborer's testimony survives. Cooperation, obligation, grief, prestige and unequal influence are all possibilities. Claims of coercion require stronger evidence than “this monument was difficult to build.”

sections.title: Celebrate discoveries, changing traditions and living continuity

items.text: Marine foods can distort radiocarbon ages because old dissolved carbon enters food webs. At Cabeçuda, paired shell, charcoal and human bone let researchers estimate and correct the reservoir effect. That detective work is an achievement: the best date is not always the number a laboratory first prints.

Geophysical surveys can reveal buried layers and hearth-like anomalies before excavation, letting teams target small areas and preserve more of a site. Non-destructive technology does not replace careful digging; it adds a map of possibilities. The mound stays mostly intact while researchers decide which questions justify disturbance.

Ancient genomes reveal that southeastern and southern mound communities were not one genetically uniform population. Contact with inland peoples increased in late periods, but ancestry is not language or culture. Genetic similarity cannot turn present Kaingang, Guarani, Laklano-Xokleng or other nations into automatic descendants of every excavated person.

Collections at Joinville preserve tools, animal remains and records from sites that lime quarrying and development damaged. Museums also inherit older collecting problems, including lost context and human remains. Preservation today should involve ethical care, transparent records and Indigenous participation, not simply locking attractive objects in cases.

In 900 the atlas removes this economic umbrella; people and coastal knowledge do not end. Late shellmounds show continuity, pottery and new relationships rather than one sudden fall. Living Kaingang cultural work is one present example, not a claim of sole succession. Every living Indigenous nation keeps its own name and history.

ending.text: The exact atlas layer contracts in 800 and disappears in 900, but no synchronized cultural fall is documented. Coastal mound traditions had already changed in different ways through fish-rich deposits, ceramics, mobility and contact. Later Indigenous histories are regionally specific, and living nations retain their own identities; the override therefore keeps fell null and invents no single successor chain.
